Maxinsights is betting there’s a big business in supplying the training material. The Santa Clara, California-based startup this week announced a $30 million seed round led by Peak XV Partners, with participation from Tola Capital, South Park Commons, Ince Capital and Alumni Ventures. The company, founded by veterans of the robotics and autonomous vehicle industries, is building what it calls the data layer for physical AI. Its approach is surprisingly low-tech in some respects: Pay people to wear cameras while they go about everyday tasks, from washing dishes to preparing food or cleaning hotel rooms. But turning all that footage into something useful for robotics models is more complicated. Maxinsights develops its own recording hardware and AI-powered software to collect, label and organize the data so robots can learn from it. The startup says it has already captured more than 2 million hours of human activity, with 1.5 million hours ready for use in AI training. Its customers include robotics model developers Genesis AI and Dyna Robotics. top_stories.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
top_stories.content: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. This is max: For comparison, I ran fresh pelicans against Kimi K3 on those three reasoning levels. items.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
items.content: OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content "without risk of affecting external systems." OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. items.title: Protecting Trade Secrets In The Age Of AI
items.content: By Seth Kugler If you only have six months of experience in an industry, you usually aren’t equipped to poach your employer’s clients and start a competing business. Of course, you may believe otherwise if you plan to use your employer’s proprietary information to train an AI agent to do the heavy lifting for you. Seth Kugler, partner at Grellas Shah LLP. That is exactly what the defendant attempted in a recent federal trade secrets case I litigated on behalf of a client in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. In that case, the defendant, a former senior employee at the marketing agency, didn’t just copy client lists to solicit accounts. Instead, he used stolen trade secrets as training inputs to build, essentially, an AI version of his old boss, attempting a shortcut to create a competing business without spending years developing the skills and expertise typically needed to provide such services. AI is creating new ways to misappropriate trade secrets, well beyond the classic theft story of an employee downloading files onto a thumb drive. This case highlights a new reality for founders, exposing unprecedented risks related to AI and trade secrets, employee use of personal devices, and the heightened need for companies to protect themselves in the age of agentic AI. Key lessons for founders AI contamination cannot be undone The defense in this case argued that because their client placed the stolen documents in a “quarantine folder” and no clients had been poached yet, no harm had been done. The court appropriately recognized that the “quarantine folder” was grossly insufficient, granting our temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction while recognizing the competing AI agent as an “existential threat.” An agreement not to touch just the stolen documents themselves is essentially irrelevant once AI gets involved: If a trade secret is used to develop a machine learning model or used to train an AI agent with recursive capabili

items.content: Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you'll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you're using personalized AI features. all_items.title: The Week’s 10 Biggest Funding Rounds: AI Drives A Varied Lineup Of Large Financings
all_items.content: Want to keep track of the largest startup funding deals in 2026 with our curated list of $100 million-plus venture deals to U.S.-based companies? Check out The Crunchbase Megadeals Board. This is a weekly feature that runs down the week’s Top 10 announced funding rounds in the U.S. Check out last week’s biggest funding deal roundup here. It was another interesting week for AI-related startup funding, with a number of large rounds and quirky companies. The largest financings went to Tenstorrent, a developer of AI processors and systems, and AI lab Flapping Airplanes. The quirkiest round, meanwhile, was undoubtedly a $200 million financing for Warhound, which wants to breed elite military dogs. A number of big rounds in areas including biotech, space tech and physical AI rounded out the list. 1. Tenstorrent, $1.5B, AI infrastructure: Santa Clara, California-based Tenstorrent, a developer of AI processors and systems, secured $1.5 billion in Series E funding. Trace Capital and Innovation X led the round, which set a $6.2 billion valuation for the 10-year-old company. 2. Flapping Airplanes, $1B, foundational AI: Flapping Airplanes, an AI lab with a focus on developing models that cost less to train and run, closed on $1 billion in Series A funding led by Lux Capital and Index Ventures. The round comes less than 10 months after the year-old San Francisco startup raised a $180 million seed financing. 3. ASI, $325M, AI for critical infrastructure: ASI, a developer of AI technology for securing and operating critical infrastructure in areas such as aviation, transportation and defense, picked up $325 million in Series C financing. Spark Capital led the round, which set a $3 billion valuation for the Boston-based company. 4. Xona, $250M, space tech: Xona, a startup developing a next-generation version of GPS, raised $250 million in Series D funding led by Future Ventures. all_items.title: 5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Robot Training, Space Lasers And Greener Cement
all_items.content: This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here. From teaching robots to do everyday household chores to using lasers to track satellites in space, this month’s crop of interesting startup deals spans some decidedly different corners of tech. Other startups that caught our eye are working on making cement production less polluting, turning agricultural waste into a useful tool for carbon removal, and helping independent video game developers get their product in front of more players. Let’s take a closer look. $30M to teach robots by watching humans Before robots can fold laundry, load dishwashers or prepare meals, they need to learn how humans actually do those things. Maxinsights is betting there’s a big business in supplying the training material. The Santa Clara, California-based startup this week announced a $30 million seed round led by Peak XV Partners, with participation from Tola Capital, South Park Commons, Ince Capital and Alumni Ventures. The company, founded by veterans of the robotics and autonomous vehicle industries, is building what it calls the data layer for physical AI. Its approach is surprisingly low-tech in some respects: Pay people to wear cameras while they go about everyday tasks, from washing dishes to preparing food or cleaning hotel rooms. But turning all that footage into something useful for robotics models is more complicated. Maxinsights develops its own recording hardware and AI-powered software to collect, label and organize the data so robots can learn from it. The startup says it has already captured more than 2 million hours of human activity, with 1.5 million hours ready for use in AI training. Its customers include robotics model developers Genesis AI and Dyna Robotics. all_items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
all_items.content: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). Here are the pelicans I got for Kimi K3.1 Pro on the three reasoning levels it supports - low, medium, and max. This is max: For comparison, I ran fresh pelicans against Kimi K3 on those three reasoning levels. all_items.title: Protecting Trade Secrets In The Age Of AI
all_items.content: By Seth Kugler If you only have six months of experience in an industry, you usually aren’t equipped to poach your employer’s clients and start a competing business. Of course, you may believe otherwise if you plan to use your employer’s proprietary information to train an AI agent to do the heavy lifting for you. Seth Kugler, partner at Grellas Shah LLP. That is exactly what the defendant attempted in a recent federal trade secrets case I litigated on behalf of a client in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. In that case, the defendant, a former senior employee at the marketing agency, didn’t just copy client lists to solicit accounts. Instead, he used stolen trade secrets as training inputs to build, essentially, an AI version of his old boss, attempting a shortcut to create a competing business without spending years developing the skills and expertise typically needed to provide such services. AI is creating new ways to misappropriate trade secrets, well beyond the classic theft story of an employee downloading files onto a thumb drive. This case highlights a new reality for founders, exposing unprecedented risks related to AI and trade secrets, employee use of personal devices, and the heightened need for companies to protect themselves in the age of agentic AI. Key lessons for founders AI contamination cannot be undone The defense in this case argued that because their client placed the stolen documents in a “quarantine folder” and no clients had been poached yet, no harm had been done. The court appropriately recognized that the “quarantine folder” was grossly insufficient, granting our temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction while recognizing the competing AI agent as an “existential threat.” An agreement not to touch just the stolen documents themselves is essentially irrelevant once AI gets involved: If a trade secret is used to develop a machine learning model or used to train an AI agent with recursive capabili
